d.t: Indicating disapproval, scoffery, irritation, impatience or disbelief.
d.e: “Let him! Dost think these simple Englishmen can ever compete with us on the high seas? Pfaff! They are like the silly sheep they raise and are only fit for shearing. […]”

d.t: Acronym of perfluoroalkyl or polyfluoroalkyl substance (“a type of environmental pollutant”).
To purl into front and back of same stitch.
d.e: Round 3: Pfb, work Row 3 of Chart A1 (A1, A1, A2, A2) twice, pfb.

d.t: One hundredth of the former German mark (Deutsche Mark).
An expression of annoyance or disappointment.
A dismissive response to a ridiculous comment.
d.e: My doctor advised me to drink less. Pff, if only it were so easy.

d.t: The sound made whilst blowing a raspberry.
Used to signify a sudden ending or disappearance.
d.e: 1965 Peter De Vries — Let Me Count the Ways You'd never forgive yourself — and then you'd never forgive me, and then pfft, the end of a fine friendship.

d.t: Used to signify sarcasm or disagreement.
d.e: “[…] You remember that lump I got? I felt something poking out of it. So I pulled, like, I just pulled one out, put it on some folded-up toilet paper, then went back in and got another one. Then one more after that. I’m pretty sure they’re spider legs,” Orvil says. ¶ “Pfffffft,”…

d.t: Used to signify a puffing sound.
The sound of a short fart.

d.e: "Are we talking a delicate little Scandinavian pfft, or the whole raspberry tart?"

d.t: A toothed machine for shredding cellulose in the manufacture of synthetic materials.
A pound (unit of weight), in German contexts.
